newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin gives liberal reformer Chubais key role.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin gives liberal reformer Chubais key role.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin appointed liberal ally Anatoly Chubais first deputy prime minister on Friday, a move likely to boost further free-market economic reforms in Russia.

The appointment of Chubais, the mastermind of the Russian government's plan to privatise state-owned assets, had been widely expected, and signals the first of a series of promised dramatic changes in the Russian government.
"The president of the Russian Federation Boris Nikolayevich Yeltsin has issued an order appointing Anatoly Borisovich Chubais first deputy prime minister," a Kremlin spokesman said.
The decree did not specify Chubais's new duties and did not mention three other men holding the same title in the cabinet.
But Kremlin sources have said Chubais, 41, was likely to become the sole person to be first deputy prime minister while the others would be demoted or sacked.
Chubais who had been serving as Yeltsin's chief of staff, is respected in the West as a dedicated reformer. He is also an excellent administrator and organiser.

"The situation in the economy is extremely complicated," Chubais told Interfax news agency on Friday evening. But "the authorities are able to overcome the negative influences in the economy and impose order in the country, first of all in the paying of wages and pensions."

Some experts said the reshuffle could free Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin from everyday running of the economy and allow him to become Yeltsin's heir-apparent for the presidential election in 2000. Chubais would be free to pursue reforms.
The highly unpopular Chubais does not seem to have any direct presidential ambitions but he is widely seen as a potential kingmaker with immense power.
Interfax said Chernomyrdin and Chubais would be given a free hand to shape a new cabinet.
Nothing could have enraged the opposition-dominated lower chamber of parliament more.
"This decision will lead to nothing other than the further worsening of the situation in the country," communist leader Gennady Zyuganov told Interfax.

The opposition hate the "Iron Chubais" for his privatisation campaign in 1992-1996 which they see as a cheap sell-off. They also despise him for his pivotal role in Yeltsin's re-election campaign in 1996.

The West is sure to hail Chubais's new role. He is trusted by the likes of the International Monetary Fund and the Group of Seven industrial nations and he is capable of reviving confidence that reforms in Russia are not stalled.

The appointment comes a day after Yeltsin, marking his return to active duty following eight months of illness, delivered a strong state of the nation speech in which he promised to reshuffle and streamline the government, install order and root out top-level corruption.
Zyuganov, who lost to Yeltsin in last July's presidential race, earlier said the communists would work for a no-confidence vote in the cabinet if Chubais were appointed.
"We will not obey any orders from Chubais, no matter what his position," he said.
If the Duma twice musters enough votes for a no-confidence move, Yeltsin would have a choice of dismissing either the government or the Duma itself.

Yeltsin also turned his attention on Friday to integration between Russia and neighbouring Belarus by welcoming its hardline president Alexander Lukashenko to the Kremlin for talks on bringing the two Slav states closer together in line with a deal they signed last April.
The two leaders signed a joint declaration that called for integration of their countries' customs, fiscal, transport and energy systems and synchronisation of economic reforms.
The declaration also said both states opposed NATO's plans to admit several former Warsaw Pact countries, probably including Belarus's neighbour Poland, later this year.
